c.tagline: City of peace and okonomiyaki, gateway to the floating torii of Miyajima.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered, plentiful, and fairly pricey; ride-hailing is limited — GO and DiDi dispatch licensed taxis rather than private cars, and Uber in Japan also only books regular taxis.

emergency.note: 110 reaches the police and 119 reaches fire and ambulance; English support is limited, so the Japan Visitor Hotline (050-3816-2787) offers 24/7 multilingual help.

hood_landmark.Peace Memorial Park (Naka): Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park A-Bomb Dome

avoid.reason: The Nagarekawa nightlife district has touts and pushy bars late at night; otherwise usual city awareness suffices.

hood_desc: The commercial heart of the city around the covered Hondori arcade and Kamiyacho, packed with department stores, restaurants, and the main streetcar interchange; the most convenient walkable base for first-timers.

The riverside civic core around the Peace Memorial Park, the A-Bomb Dome, and the Peace Memorial Museum, with wide boulevards and Hiroshima Castle nearby; best for travelers who want the must-see sights on their doorstep.
Hiroshima's main entertainment district, a dense grid of izakayas, bars, clubs, and okonomiyaki joints that comes alive after dark; suits night owls and diners.
The area around Hiroshima Station and the Shinkansen, a fast-modernizing hub of hotels, the ekie shopping complex, and easy connections; convenient for arrivals and day-trippers.

Yokogawa is an old shitamachi neighbourhood around JR and streetcar Yokogawa Station in Nishi Ward, about 5 minutes by train from Hiroshima Station, with a shopping street of 180-plus stores, a retro cinema and local bars. It suits travellers wanting a cheaper, lived-in base with good links, though hotel choice is thin and the main sights need a tram ride.
lodging: Hiroshima Peace Hotel (HIROSHIMAピースホテル)

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Japan.

transit.hours: Hiroden streetcars and city buses run from around 5:30 AM to about 11:00 PM; the Astram Line keeps similar hours, and there is no night service, so late trips fall to taxis.
transit.note: Hiroshima's signature transit is the Hiroden streetcar (tram) network — one of Japan's largest surviving tram systems — backed by an extensive city bus network, the elevated Astram Line people-mover, JR local trains, and ferries across the bay to Miyajima.
transit.pay: Tap a nationwide IC card (ICOCA, Suica, or Hiroshima's own MOBIRY DAYS) or a contactless credit card on trams and buses; a flat streetcar ride in the city is about ¥190 (~US$1.30). Cash and paper tickets are also accepted onboard.

transit.m: Airport Limousine Bus to Hiroshima Station (~50 min)
Airport Limousine Bus to Hiroshima Bus Center / Peace Park (~65 min)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in Japan and can cause confusion; excellent service is standard and already included.

food.name: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki
food.desc: Layered not mixed: thin crepe, a mountain of cabbage, pork belly, fried noodles and egg, pressed on the griddle and painted with sweet sauce.

places.name: Mitchan Souhonten
places.note: The founding house of the layered noodle style, running since 1950; counter seats face the griddle.

places.name: Okonomimura
places.note: Four floors of about two dozen competing okonomiyaki stalls; mostly cash only, so bring yen.

places.name: Nagataya
places.note: Popular polished version with shrimp and squid tempura; expect a queue at lunch.

food.name: Hiroshima oysters
food.desc: Hiroshima Bay grows roughly two thirds of Japan's oysters. Eaten grilled in the shell, deep fried as kaki fry, or simmered in miso hotpot.

places.name: Kakiya
places.note: Oyster specialist minutes from the Miyajima ferry pier; grilled, fried and raw on one menu.

places.name: Yakigaki no Hayashi
places.note: Long-running charcoal-grilled oyster house on the island's main approach street.

places.name: Kanawa
places.note: Oyster restaurant moored on a barge on the river; the refined sit-down version.

food.name: Hiroshima tsukemen
food.desc: Chilled noodles with cabbage and pork dipped in a cold, fiery sesame, soy and chilli sauce. Heat is ordered by number, and the top levels hurt.

places.name: Bakudanya
places.note: The best-known chain for the local style; start around level 3 unless you like real chilli.

places.name: Hiroshima Tsukemen Ryushanhai
places.note: Credited with inventing the Hiroshima dipping-noodle style; small, no-frills counter shop.

food.name: Anago meshi
food.desc: Saltwater conger eel from the Seto Inland Sea, grilled with a light sweet glaze and laid over rice cooked in the eel bones' broth.

places.name: Anagomeshi Ueno
places.note: Serving the dish since 1901; also sells the famous boxed version to take on the ferry.

places.name: Fujitaya
places.note: Island institution grilling anago to order; limited daily portions, so go early.

food.name: Momiji manju
food.desc: Maple-leaf shaped sponge cakes filled with red bean, custard or cheese. On Miyajima look for age-momiji, the deep-fried version on a skewer.

places.name: Momijido
places.note: Century-old maker best known for age-momiji, the battered deep-fried version eaten hot.

places.name: Takatsudo
places.note: The shop where the cake was invented in 1906, eight minutes from the ferry terminal.

places.name: Daikonya
places.note: Watch the cakes come off the moulds and eat them still warm.

food.name: Hiroshima ramen
food.desc: A gentler local bowl than the big-name styles: cloudy soy and pork broth, thin straight noodles, plenty of bean sprouts and spring onion.

places.name: Chuka Soba Kunimatsu
places.note: Long-standing shop pouring the classic clear soy version locals grew up on.

places.name: Shukaen
places.note: Old Chinese restaurant whose ramen is a Hiroshima cult favourite; cash and patience needed.

places.name: Ekie Ramen area
places.note: Several local ramen counters under one roof, handy before a shinkansen.

food.name: Hiroshima sake
food.desc: Saijo, half an hour east, is one of Japan's three great sake towns; its soft-water brewing gives a rounder, sweeter sake than Kobe or Kyoto styles.

places.name: Sakagura-dori
places.note: Street of red-brick chimneys and about seven working breweries offering tastings.

places.name: Kamotsuru Brewery
places.note: Historic house with a tasting room; its gold-flake daiginjo is the famous bottle.

places.name: Ekie
places.note: Sake stands and shops pouring prefecture labels by the glass without leaving the city.

food.name: Setouchi lemon drinks
food.desc: The Inland Sea islands grow most of Japan's lemons, turned into lemon sours, sparkling lemonade and lemon soft-serve floats all over the city.

places.name: Miyajima Omotesando
places.note: Stalls squeezing lemon soda and lemon soft serve along the shrine approach.

places.name: Hondori arcade
places.note: Cafes and izakaya on the covered shopping street pour lemon sours made with island fruit.

places.name: Ekie
places.note: Setouchi lemon drinks, syrups and bottled sours in one place for the road.

landmarks: Atomic Bomb Dome (Genbaku Dome)
The skeletal UNESCO-listed dome left standing near the 1945 hypocenter endures as the world's most powerful architectural plea for peace.
Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park and Cenotaph
A riverside park of memorials, the eternal Flame of Peace and the arched cenotaph framing the Dome invites quiet reflection at the city's heart.
Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum
Harrowing personal artifacts and testimony convey the human reality of the atomic bombing, an essential, profoundly moving visit for every traveler.
Itsukushima Shrine and the Floating Torii (Miyajima)
A short ferry away, the vermilion torii gate rising from the tides before a UNESCO-listed shrine ranks among Japan's three most celebrated views.
Children's Peace Monument
Thousands of rainbow-hued paper cranes surround this statue of Sadako Sasaki, the leukemia-stricken girl whose origami became a global symbol of peace.
Hiroshima Castle (Carp Castle)
A faithful reconstruction of the 1590s keep rises from its moat amid a tree-filled compound, housing a samurai museum with top-floor city views.
Shukkei-en Garden
This 1620 'shrunken scenery' garden miniaturizes lakes, valleys and tea pavilions around a carp pond, a tranquil Edo-era escape near the station.
Mount Misen (Miyajima)
Hike or ride the ropeway up Miyajima's sacred peak, past wild deer and Kobo Daishi's eternally burning flame, to a spectacular Seto Inland Sea panorama.
Okonomimura
Three floors packed with two dozen griddle stalls serve Hiroshima's layered okonomiyaki pancake, the city's beloved soul food sizzling before your eyes.
Mitaki-dera Temple
Hidden in a maple-forested valley with three waterfalls, this mossy temple with its vermilion pagoda offers Hiroshima's most atmospheric off-the-beaten-path escape.

train.note: Japan has no international trains. Hiroshima Station is a major San'yo Shinkansen stop: Okayama is 35 minutes away, Shin-Osaka 80-85 minutes and Tokyo about 3 hours 45 minutes on a Nozomi. Japan Rail Pass holders cannot ride Nozomi or Mizuho without paying a surcharge of roughly Y6,500 and should take a Hikari instead, which stretches the Tokyo trip to about 4 hours 30 minutes. Conventional JR lines and the city's tram network run from the same station, and for Miyajima you take a Sanyo Line local to Miyajimaguchi.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Japan. Long-distance coaches use the north exit of JR Hiroshima Station and the Hiroshima Bus Center on the third floor of the SOGO department store in the centre. The overnight New Breeze to Tokyo is run by JR Chugoku Bus with Odakyu City Bus (about Y13,250, or Y7,700 booked early), JR Bus runs frequent daytime services to Kyoto and Osaka for Y3,500-4,500, and Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) sells Tokyo seats from about Y7,700 and Kyoto/Osaka day runs from Y4,600 online in English.

intl.to: Matsuyama (Japan) - sails from Hiroshima Port Ujina passenger terminal, about 25 min by tram from the centre
Miyajima (Japan) - high-speed boat from Ujina and from the Peace Memorial Park pier
Kure and Etajima (Japan) - sails from Hiroshima Port Ujina passenger terminal

ferry.note: Hiroshima has no international sailings, but Ujina is one of the busiest domestic ferry ports on the Inland Sea. The Superjet hydrofoil reaches Matsuyama on Shikoku in 70-80 minutes for about Y6,980, while the slower cruise ferry takes 2 hours 40 minutes for about Y3,670 - both are run by Setonaikai Kisen with Ishizaki Kisen. Boats also serve Miyajima, Kure and Etajima, and the classic route to Miyajima is the short JR Miyajima Ferry crossing from Miyajimaguchi, which is covered by the Japan Rail Pass. Cruise-ferry departures have been thinned out in recent years because of fuel costs, so check the timetable before relying on a late sailing.

half.name: Onomichi
half.blurb: Hillside port town of narrow lanes and temples, and the starting point of the Shimanami Kaido cycling route.

half.name: Kure
half.blurb: Former Imperial Japanese Navy port with a museum housing artifacts from the battleship Yamato.

half.name: Iwakuni
half.blurb: Home to the Kintai Bridge, a five-arched wooden bridge spanning the Nishiki River below a hilltop castle.

half.name: Miyajima (Itsukushima)
half.blurb: Sacred island famed for Itsukushima Shrine's floating torii, hikes up Mount Misen and free-roaming deer.

full.name: Tomonoura
full.blurb: Small port town of Edo-era streets and a stone lantern lighthouse, said to have inspired scenes in Studio Ghibli films.
